comparison: Both evaluations support the core methodological contribution (C3, C5, C22, C23, C27, C122). OpenEval provides detailed technical validation citing equations and simulations, while peer reviewers affirm the method's solid evidence and meaningful contribution to normative modeling. OpenEval additionally evaluates C4, C47, C48 not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Complete agreement on claim coverage (C92, C93, C106-C112). However, evaluations diverge: OpenEval rates these clinical correlations as UNCERTAIN due to non-significant p-values (p=0.06), unexpected negative relationships, and speculative interpretations, while peer reviewers rate them as SUPPORTED without raising statistical concerns.

Perfect agreement on cross-sectional findings (C7, C89, C90). Both evaluations support these results. OpenEval explicitly validates the statistical methods (Mann-Whitney U with FDR correction), while peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as valid context for longitudinal analysis.

Complete agreement on preprocessing validation (C86, C87, C88). Both evaluations support the robustness findings across preprocessing methods. OpenEval emphasizes the power advantage of longitudinal preprocessing, while peer reviewers focus on practical utility given cross-sectional model availability.

Perfect agreement on acknowledged limitations (C116-C121). Both evaluations support the authors' self-critique. OpenEval characterizes this as demonstrating 'appropriate scientific caution,' while peer reviewers view the limitations as reasonable given the methodological advance.

Strong agreement on literature contextualization (C94-C104). Both support the authors' interpretation of unexpected findings through recent literature. OpenEval validates the appropriately qualified speculation about compensatory mechanisms, while peer reviewers accept the contextualization without challenge. OpenEval uniquely addresses C105.

Both address primary clinical findings (C8, C9, C91, C124) and support them. OpenEval notes the contradiction with historical expectations requiring careful interpretation, while peer reviewers emphasize the solid evidence for the new methods. OpenEval uniquely evaluates C115 (ANCOVA comparison) in this result, which peer reviewers address separately.

Both evaluate comparative evidence for methodological advantages (C113, C114). Complete agreement in supporting these claims. OpenEval provides detailed validation of ANCOVA covariates and multiple comparison correction, while peer reviewers endorse the demonstration of z-diff method's superior sensitivity. OpenEval additionally addresses C115.

Both address clinical dataset and study procedures (C58-C69). Strong overlap with additional claims in peer review (C4, C6, C33-C35, C70, C71, C75, C76). Both support these methodological details. OpenEval focuses on dataset characteristics and ethical procedures, while peer reviewers broadly accept data adequacy and preprocessing methods.

Both address methodological rationale (C14, C15, C21, C24, C25). Complete agreement in supporting these claims. OpenEval validates the rationale through citations and acknowledges the distinction from true longitudinal models, while peer reviewers explicitly validate the meaningfulness of addressing the gap between cross-sectional models and longitudinal inference.

Partial overlap on theoretical distinctions (C18, C19, C20). OpenEval evaluates C17-C20 as supported, emphasizing the importance of distinguishing 'trajectory of distributions' vs. 'distribution over trajectories.' Peer review R7 addresses these claims within broader methodological motivation (C14-C25) without specific commentary on theoretical distinctions.

Both address pre-trained models (C33, C34, C35, C76). OpenEval supports these as factual statements about published models with appropriate citations. Peer review R2 addresses these within broader acceptance of data and methods adequacy without raising specific concerns.

Both address preprocessing procedures (C70, C71, C75). OpenEval supports the dual preprocessing approach and quality control protocols. Peer review R2 includes these claims within broader acceptance of preprocessing methods and data adequacy without specific concerns.

Minimal overlap on C26. OpenEval rates C16 and C26 as UNCERTAIN due to apparent contradiction about cross-sectional models' ability to capture longitudinal variance. Peer review R1 includes C26 within supported methodological contribution without addressing the tension OpenEval identifies.

OpenEval evaluates theoretical assumptions (C38-C41, C44-C45) as SUPPORTED, noting the authors' explicit acknowledgment of assumptions and appropriate scientific rigor. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific theoretical assumptions.

OpenEval evaluates analytical pipeline (C77, C79-C83) as SUPPORTED, validating statistical methods including Wilcoxon test, ANCOVA, PCA, and FDR correction. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing the analytical pipeline, though methods are implicitly accepted.

OpenEval evaluates practical considerations in normative modeling (C28, C29) as SUPPORTED, noting availability of pre-trained models as key enabler. No corresponding peer review evaluation found specifically addressing these practical considerations.

OpenEval evaluates clinical application description (C6) as SUPPORTED, noting modest but reasonable sample size. Peer review R2 includes C6 within broader dataset acceptance but does not provide specific evaluation of the clinical application claim.
